ITT Questions – Lot 2 HMP/YOI Winchester 
 
The category column identifies whether a question is a ‘Core’ or ‘Lot Specific’ question.  
Core questions are applicable to both Lots and Bidders are required to answer these questions once, regardless of whether applying for one or both Lots.   
Lot Specific questions apply to each individual Lot and Bidders are required to submit separate answers to these questions for each Lot applied for. 
Please refer to the ITT Bidder Instructions C.9 for further information.

Lot Specific 
 
 
 
Please describe your  overarching management structure and service delivery model for HMP/YOI Winchester , setting out your key 
organisational principles that support an integrated, trauma-informed health and wellbeing service and how you will deliver all elements of the 
service specification(s) to achieve the required outcomes. 
 
Please refer to the Service Specification(s), Desktop Health and Social Care Needs Assessment, and Information Pack included in the ITT 
documentation. 
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Describe which elements of the service specification(s) you will deliver directly. 
• Explain where and how you will subcontract and collaborate with specialist partners to deliver each aspect of the service specifications, 
as a single, integrated service model, including how partners will be selected, managed, and how quality and performance will be  
monitored. 
• Describe how your service model will adapt and develop to meet the changing profile of the prison population and future growth, not 
limited to, including any transition measures: 
o Changes in National Policy 
o Drug Strategy Policy 
o National Prison Expansion Programme. 
• Describe your approach to implementing an early days in custody strategy. 
 
Please provide as an attachment an overarching service delivery model diagram  and your organisational management structure . 
N.B. This attachment must be pictorial in nature and may include minimal narrative as appropriate to ensure it remains in line with 
A.12.19 of the ITT Bidder Instructions.

Lot Specific 
Please describe your strategy for demand management and explain your approach to providing services over the duration of the contract in 
order to meet the requirements of the service specification(s).  
 
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Your approach to planning, capacity management, staffing availability (including subcontractors) and contingency arrangements to 
manage fluctuating demand, including surge management, increased churn, and how service user data and intelligence will be used 
to inform your approach.   
• Your proposed programme of clinics/sessions, including GP provision, and how this meets the service standards, for each service 
listed in the service specification(s). 
• How the services will be made available within HMP/YOI Winchester’s core day. Include the operating hours, evenings, weekends 
and out of hours provision, and 24-hour cover as applicable. 
• How you will maximise healthcare clinic utilisation, manage referrals, and reduce Did Not Attends (DNAs). 
• Your strategies to reduce the demand for community-based and acute health provision, as well as relevant processes to access 
appropriate community-based services.  
• How workforce and health resources, including technology (e.g. telemedicine), will be strategically utilised to ensure appropriate 
service availability. 
 
Please provide as an attachment a list of draft clinic/session plans for HMP/YOI Winchester. N.B. This attachment may include 
minimal narrative as appropriate to ensure it remains in line with A.12.19 of the ITT Bidder Instructions.

With reference to the Service Specification(s), Desktop Health and Social Care Needs Assessment and Information Pack provided as part of 
the ITT documentation, please describe how reception services will be delivered to meet the specific requirements and challenges of service 
provision at HMP/YOI Winchester. 
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Your reception staffing profile, including roles, WTEs, deployment patterns, and evening, night and weekend cover. 
• Your approach to initial assessment, including access, language needs, mental and physical health, substance misuse, medication, 
duration of assessment, risk management, and onward care planning. 
• How appropriate screening and pathways will be put in place for those service users who have specific needs, including long-term 
conditions, ADHD and autism. 
• How you will manage late receptions and short-notice surges in arrivals at HMP/YOI Winchester. 
 
Please provide as an attachment a draft reception pathway for arrivals at HMP/YOI Winchester. N.B. This attachment must be

Lot Specific 
 
 
With reference to the relevant service specification and Desktop Health and Social Care Needs Assessment provided, please describe your 
trauma informed substance misuse service delivery model for HMP/YOI Winchester and how it will meet the needs of the population. 
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Describe how your delivery model can incorporate the needs of residents appropriate to their length of stay at HMP/YOI Winchester 
and will effectively provide rapid access to essential clinical and psychosocial substance misuse services. 
• How you will deliver safe and clinically effective treatment programmes, including Opiate Substitute Therapy (OST) 
initiation/continuation and prescribing governance. 
• How you will work with service users and tailor your approach for different cultural backgrounds and those with protected 
characteristics (including learning difficulties) to reduce harm from all types of alcohol and drug misuse, including the management of 
previously unmet need and dual diagnosis. 
• How you will ensure sufficient, appropriately skilled staffing is available at all times to meet the substance misuse specification.

Mental Health 
 
Lot Specific 
 
With reference to the relevant service specification and Desktop Health and Social Care Needs Assessment provided, please describe your 
trauma-informed mental health service delivery model for HMP/YOI Winchester and how it meets the needs of the population.  
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• How your delivery model will flex to meet fluctuating demand for mental health support and ensure patients have access to low-level 
interventions and a range of psychological therapies. 
• How service users, in particular with learning difficulties and other neurodiverse vulnerabilities will be identified and supported to 
ensure that their health needs are met, including identifying those with a history of trauma, physical impairments, and broader 
cognitive impairments. 
• How you will ensure timely triage and assessment following referral, including prioritisation and rapid response for individuals at risk 
of self-harm/suicide.  
• How you will deliver mental health care within the In Patient Unit (IPU) at HMP/YOI Winchester as part of your integrated health 
model, including recovery interventions.

Lot Specific 
 
Please describe how dental services will be provided in a trauma informed way at HMP/YOI Winchester to ensure effective and maximised 
delivery of assessments, planned and emergency/urgent treatments.  
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to:  
 
• How assessments and planned care will be delivered based on clinical need and aligned to length of detention. 
• How service users will be supported to maintain dental hygiene and self-care following treatment.  
• How emergency / urgent treatments will be screened and managed, including during out-of-hours. 
• Your quality assurance processes e.g., Radiography, Infection Prevention and Control. 
 
Please note - If the prime provider cannot hold a PDS contract, NHS England will enter into a PDS contract with the dental services 
provider who forms part of the prime provider’s bid. In this case a tripartite agreement will be necessary between the prime 
provider, the dental services provider and NHS England. Payments for dental services, which will be determined between the 
Prime provider and Dental Contractor, will be made directly to the dental Contractor on a fixed cost by NHSE via COMPASS but 
accountability for the management of the dental service will remain with the prime provider.

Public Health  
 
Lot Specific 
With reference to the Service Specification(s) and Desktop Health and Social Care Needs Assessment provided, please describe your 
overall public health strategy for HMP/YOI Winchester and how public health programmes and objectives will be embedded in all elements 
of healthcare delivery.  
 
Responses should consider current national evidence on the health needs of people in prison, including prevention, health inequalities, 
ageing and increasingly complex populations, and continuity of care. 
  
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
  
• How population health intelligence, public health needs assessment findings and service data will be used to identify priority groups, 
unmet need and variation in access and outcomes. 
• How key public health programmes, including Section 7A screening programmes, will be delivered both planned and 
opportunistically, taking account of population movement such as reception, transfer and release. 
• How public health delivery will be integrated into care, including Making Every Contact Count and joint working with partner 
organisations where relevant, through effective co-ordination e.g., HMPPS, education, and community providers. 
• How you will deliver integrated health promotion programmes that support self-management of long-term conditions, including the 
use of peers and service user representatives to support health promotion. 
• How health inequalities will be identified and addressed to ensure access according to need, including for under-reported and/or 
protected characteristics, and for older people or those with increasing complexity.

Please describe how you will engage and work with key internal and external stakeholders to deliver effective healthcare at HMP/YOI 
Winchester. 
 
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Identify the key stakeholders you will work with (including the HMPPS, Local Authority, Community Providers, etc), and how and why 
you will engage with them to achieve positive health outcomes for service users. 
• How risks arising from ineffective stakeholder engagement will be identified and managed. 
• How partnership issues will be escalated internally within HMP/YOI Winchester and externally where required. 
• How you will collaborate with partners to support care pathways commissioned through other routes (e.g. Social Care, Mental Health 
Transfers, Offender Personality Disorder Pathways, RECONNECT, Community Sexual Health Services including SARCs, and 
Community Drug and Alcohol Services).

Lot Specific 
Please describe your proposed pathways for effective continuation of care on release into the community and on transfer to another secure 
establishment (Prisons or Secure Hospitals).   
 
Your response must include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• How internal and external healthcare pathways (as applicable) will support continuity of care for service users as they leave prison 
for transfer to another secure estate. 
• How you will ensure seamless access to healthcare for service users released into the community, including those with ongoing 
medical conditions (e.g. physical, mental, substance misuse). 
• How you will establish and manage partnerships (e.g. Probations Services, HMPPS, RECONNECT and relevant local community-
based services) to support successful community resettlement, prevent homelessness and reduce the likelihood of re-offending.  
• How your pathways will support service users subject to short-notice release or transfer.

Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• How you will promote physical and mental health and wellbeing for your staff, particularly those who experience health inequalities or 
multiple vulnerabilities. 
• How your approach will support staff wellbeing, resilience, and retention in a challenging and secure environment. 
• How you will measure and monitor the impact of your social value commitments on health and wellbeing.

Lot Specific 
Please describe how the integrated healthcare service will ensure safe and effective prescribing, dispensing, administration and 
management of medicines at HMP/YOI Winchester in line with the five domains of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society Professional 
Standards for Optimising Medicines for People in Secure Environments. 
 
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Safe medicines management systems and processes, including out-of-hours access, dispensing, transport, handling, return and 
disposal of controlled drugs. 
• Medicines management governance, including roles, responsibilities and oversight. 
• Medicines optimisation and patient self-care. 
• Measures to prevent misuse and diversion of medicines. 
• Continuity of medicines on transfer, discharge and deportation. 
• Staff competency frameworks, including prescribing, medicine administration and proficiency with SystmOne. 
• Communication support for service users to support patient safety and adherence.

Please describe how you will safeguard vulnerable adults and young people at risk by meeting the requirements of appropriate legislation and 
guidance. Where possible, please provide examples. 
 
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Your safeguarding leadership structure and governance arrangements, including executive and named professional roles. 
• Your safe recruitment processes. 
• How staff will be trained, supported, and supervised to identify and respond to safeguarding concerns. 
• Your processes for managing, tracking, and escalating safeguarding concerns, demonstrating awareness of the range of 
safeguarding issues within a secure environment. 
• How your safeguarding policy complies with appropriate legislation and guidance, including but not limited to the Care Act 2014, 
Mental Capacity Act 2005, intercollegiate safeguarding training requirements, and alignment with local Safeguarding Adults Boards 
and Safeguarding Children Partnerships. 
• How your safeguarding arrangements will integrate with and comply with the HMPPS safeguarding policies and responsibilities and 
how you will work in partnership with HMPPS safeguarding teams to safeguard individuals. 
• How safeguarding performance will be monitored, including board oversight, audit processes, learning, and training compliance.

Please describe your proposed staffing structures and management arrangements, for all services listed in the service specification(s) to

Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Your staffing structures, including subcontractors, demonstrating appropriate skill mix, roles, responsibilities, and WTEs. 
• Accountability and reporting arrangements. 
• How rota coverage will be maintained, including contingency arrangements for planned and unplanned leave, and how staffing 
resources will be flexed to meet changing demand and workforce development. 
• How practitioner expertise, knowledge and level of qualification will be reviewed and maintained to meet identified needs and ensure 
robust coverage of key areas of service delivery.  
• How appropriate clinical oversight and leadership will be provided. 
• Out-of-hours, on-call, and management cover arrangements. 
• How staff, including subcontractors, will be supported to contribute to an integrated healthcare service.

Please describe your approach to recruiting, developing and retaining a skilled and resilient workforce for the establishments.  
 
Your response may include, but need not be limited to: 
 
• Your recruitment and retention strategy, including continuity of staffing, minimising vacancies, managing turnover, and mitigations to 
minimise agency use. 
• How your organisation will approach TUPE, including engagement with existing workforce and management of any redundancies.  
• How your approach promotes equal opportunities, prevents discrimination and supports diversity and inclusion across all staff 
groups. 
• How you will actively recruit, support and retain staff with lived experience, and how their experience will be embedded meaningfully 
within service delivery. 
• Pre- and post-employment identity and verification checks, including Disclosure and Barring Service (BDS) requirements. 
• Your induction process, and how this will cover mandatory training, safeguarding, security awareness and the needs of the prison 
population.

1 Purpose 
This is the Service Specification for HMP / YOI Winchester integrated Custodial Healthcare 
Services. The purpose of this document is to assist Commissioners and Providers to deliver 
high-quality healthcare in prison settings  to best meet the needs of their local populations.  
This specification sets out exactly what service is being commissioned, how it should be 
delivered, and what outcomes it must achieve. 
This document is also supported by  five National Service Specification (s) for Integrated 
Custodial Healthcare; Primary Care, Dentistry, Mental Health, Substance Misuse Services  
and Specification 29 Section 7A: Public Health services for children and adults in secure and 
detained settings in England.  
2 Foreword 
Delivering high-quality healthcare in prison settings is both a moral imperative and a public 
health opportunity. Patients residing in prison must have, as a minimum, access to the same 
or equivalent range of interventions and quality of healthcare interventions as patients residing 
in the community. 
 
To ensure services remain equivalent to the community, are proportionate and effective, 
commissioners and providers must use the Health & Social Needs Assessments (HSNA) and 
a suite of data and intelligence collected nationally and locally in partnership w ith HMPPS, 
UKHSA, DHSC, and local partners and stakeholders, informing tailored local public health and 
health interventions for each site, as a foundation for decision-making.  
 
Additionally, Commissioners, Heads of each prison healthcare team, prison Governors, lived 
experience representatives, HMPPS, Integrated Care Boards and Local Authorities must work 
in partnership to meet the needs of the patients in our care , to address new and emergent 
needs and wider healthcare needs. 
 
Integration and partnership working is a core principle of this specification. Healthcare in 
custody must not operate in isolation, partnership working is an essential component of all 
custodial healthcare service specifications. It should be embedded within the wider ecosystem 
of prison operations, community health systems, and resettlement services. 
 
By adopting this stepped, patient -centred approach, we aim to improve health outcomes, 
reduce inequalities, and support safer transitions back into the community, ultimately, 
contributing to better lives, safer societies and a reduction in reoffending.

3 The model 
This service specification is structured  to enable the flexible use of the following c oncepts 
presented through four main considerations: 
 
 
• At its centre – a core framework that clearly outlines the required objectives, outcomes 
and standards of the service and the expected minimum levels of governance. 
 
• An overarching guiding principle , that defines the basis upon which activities in the 
specification are delivered ( i.e. safe, patient centred, integral peer approaches, and 
provided within a cohesive multi-disciplinary framework). The guiding principal element of 
the specification will also include signposting towards pre -existing reviews and 
recommendations.  
 
Localised elements of the specification 
 
• Full account of the setting within which delivery takes place  should be taken, especially 
where this impacts on the type or duration of intervention that can be offered (e.g. reception 
prison, training prison, resettlement prison). 
 
• A thorough examination of need, including (but not limited to) quantitative analysis, 
consultation and patient involvement. A comprehensive understanding of need is a cross-
cutting issue across al l elements of the specification.  The flexibility offered by this 
specification places the emphasis on an establishment-based service designed around 
the needs of the population, as evidenced through needs assessment. 
 
The specification and implementation provide an important opportunity to consider: 
 
• the changing profile of people in prison, such as the aging population

4 Introduction 
The 2012 Health and Social Care Act mandates NHS England (NHSE) to commission health 
services across prisons and other places of prescribed detention. As such, this specification 
describes the required degree of healthcare services that need to be delivered in these 
environments, ensuring that the principle of ‘ equivalence’ is a dhered to, enabling patients’ 
access to physical and mental health care as required  in line with services offered in the 
community, working towards agreed health outcomes and being supported to manage their 
ongoing health care needs. 
The Health and Care Act (2022) also established Integrated Healthcare Boards  (ICB), they 
are responsible for Planning and arranging NHS services, allocating budgets and oversight of 
performance and quality of community services, they now act as the main system for strategic 
commissioning, focusing on population health, integration, and reducing inequalities. As such 
prison teams must work with and align services and pathways of their local Integrated Care 
System (ICS). 
This service specification outlines what should be i ncluded in a healthcare service being 
offered to patient populations in secure and detained environments. It also includes guidance 
for the support that should be offered to individuals with learning disabil ities and other 
vulnerabilities. The Custodial Healthcare Service is also in tegrated with Primary Care, 
Dentistry, Ophthalmology, Mental Health, Substance Misuse Services, P ublic Health and 
other health support provisions (as per the specific specifications detailing required provision 
for these areas). 
There are numerous clinical guidelines and best practice documentation that describe clinical 
practice and processes to steer best practice in the delivery of physical healthcare for people 
in secure and detained environments.  This document does not aim to replicate these

People in secure and detained environments may require additional health and social care

arrangements and therefore the detail for this lies outside the scope of this specification, there 
is a strong need to work collaboratively with local authorities’ social care teams , ICB’s and

Appropriate support must be provided to people in secure and detained environments with an 
identified or suspected learning disability or difficulty to enable them to cope better within the 
secure environment and ensure that their health needs are met. The service provider also has 
a role in providing general support and advising other agencies within a prison of their 
respective responsibilities to support patients in daily life.  
For ease of reference, throughout this document the term ‘learning disability’, unless otherwise 
stated, encompasses individuals with learning disabilities  (LDs) or other vulnerabilities. It is 
recognised that neurodiversity often overlaps with learning disabilities, but they do describe 
different aspects of cognitive variation and should also be considered throughout the following 
document. 
A safe and secure prison system cannot be successfully de livered without effective primary 
care and learning disability services, in turn, such services cannot be delivered without the full 
support and partnership of the prison regime and its staff. Both the physical environment within 
which a person lives and receives care and the service provided cont ribute towards general 
physical and mental wellbeing within the prison.   
This specification aims to build upon existing positive relationships between healthcare 
services, the prison services and patients and the vast body of work  already successfully in 
place. 
It is recognised that this is a significant time of change and transition in terms of NHS and 
criminal justice system (CJS) reforms, prison reconfiguration and commissioning pathways , 
therefore elements of this specification may  be subject to review in response to variations .  
NHSE and H is Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS) commissioners will fully 
engage with the service provider during the initial service co -design period and then for the 
lifetime of the contract to ensure this specification remains relevant and meets the need s of 
the population.  
5 Guiding principle 
The purpose of health care in prison is to provide an excellent, safe and effective service to 
all patients ensuring access  to and the quality of services delivered is of  an equivalent 
standard to that of the community . Services should meet the objectives and outcomes of  
national frameworks and priorities and are expected to develop and implement measures to 
monitor these outcomes.1 
 
Services should operate from a position of ‘Making Every Contact Count’. Wherever a patient 
presents to any health service, or via some other intervention, it is incumbent upon providers 
to meet immediate needs and bring appropriate provision to the patient, not ‘send’ the patient 
to another intervention.

appropriate and address the wide range of other, often related menta l and/ or substance

Care should be person centred and delivered by professionals and allied staff who are suitably 
competent, well led, properly supervised and operating within a clear quality and clinical 
governance framework supporting safe and effective delivery. 
 
Treatment and care plans should be regularly reviewed. There should be access to suitable 
psychosocial and clinical interventions, as well as a focus on health promotion and supporting 
positive health and well-being. Where medication is indicated, its provision should be suitably 
safe particularly in those with difficulties achieving stability and with clear shared care between 
prescribers.  
Clinicians should be able to adapt evidence -based treatments from the wider community to 
the prison estate and regime and be able to work with security staff and systems to reduce 
harm and to manage risk, particularly the risk of fatalities and self -inflicted harm, as well as 
other risks to consider such as abuse and exploitation. They should also have established 
links with social care providers serving the prison and contacts with the education provider for 
the establishment to ensure those with social care and/or  communication needs receive a 
holistic package of care and support. 
Cross referencing commissioning responsibilities outside those of health and justice. 
There are several areas where the commissioning for delivering care must work in conjunction 
with the commissioning responsibilities of other areas within NHSE and where health and 
justice direct commissioning processes must be aligned.  These include services 
commissioned by specialised commissioning to our patient population constituting services 
such as anti-libidinal medication, supporting patients with serious mental health needs which 
ultimately require secure hospital care, care and treatment of specific blood borne viruses 
(BBV) conditions such as HIV infection and  the specialist treatment a transgender patient 
would require as well as supporting the social care requirements of a patient (this is not an 
exhaustive list). 
This specification describes the requirement NHSE has to commission healthcare services 
across the secure estate. This specification does not stand alone and should be considered 
in relation to other specifications and healthcare duties across the health and justice 
landscape. 
6 Policy Context 
The Provider must be aware of, consider and refer to the national and local policy context 
and drivers in the development, design and delivery of healthcare services for prisoners.   
 
The key documents are referred to below and the Provider should keep abreast of 
subsequent and updated policies and consider any relevant policies not listed. 
6.1 National Policy Drivers: 
Healthcare services within prisons are currently commissioned by NHS England (NHSE) and 
delivered within a complex, multi-agency policy framework. This is underpinned by a statutory 
and strategic partnership between the Department of Health and Social Care  (DHSC), HM 
Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), Ministry of Justice (MoJ), NHS England and the UK

Health Security Agency (UKHSA), formalised through the National Partnership Agreement for 
Health and Social Care 2022–2025.  
 
This agreement sets out a shared commitment to improving the quality, safety and 
effectiveness of health and social care services for people in prison and those on probation, 
with a strong emphasis on joint accountability, partnership working and integrate d delivery 
across custody and the community. The strategic direction for prison healthcare is set out in 
the NHS England publication, Health and Justice Framework for Integration 2022 –2025 – 
“Improving Lives, Reducing Inequality.” This framework supersedes the previous 2016–2020 
strategy, articulating a renewed national vision for the delivery of healthcare within the criminal 
justice system. Framework, vision and priorities reducing health inequalities, ensuring 
equivalent healthcare to the wider community, delivering inclusive and trauma-informed care, 
supporting continuity as individuals move between custody and the community, improving 
outcomes for those with complex needs , preventing avoidable deaths, embedding lived 
experience in service design, and driving quality improvement through digital innovation and 
data. Integration and Partnership Working framework places particular emphasis on 
integration with wider health systems (ICSs), and on partnership working across justice, health 
and social care sectors. This collaborative approach is essential for delivering joined -up, 
effective healthcare service s that address the complex needs of the prison population and 
support their rehabilitation and wellbeing. 
 
The current National Partnership Agreement 2022–2025 (NPA) builds on earlier agreements 
(2013, 2015, 2018 –21) and reflects a more mature, system -wide approach. Key priorities 
include: Improving physical and mental health outcomes for people in prison and on probation 
Addressing significant health inequalities exp erienced by this population strengthening joint 
governance, accountability and assurance arrangements across partner organisations 
supporting integrated commissioning and service delivery models enhancing data sharing, 
population health management and evidence-based commissioning, responding to emerging 
risks including communicable diseases, ageing prison populations and complex comorbidities. 
The agreement explicitly extends beyond custody to include probation and community 
pathways, supporting a whole-system, end-to-end care model. 
 
The national policy direction for prison healthcare, continues to place emphasis on the need 
to address health inequalities, deliver high -quality care equivalent to that available in the 
community, and strengthen integration across custody, probation, and community services. It 
also highlights the importance of person -centred care, robust safety and governance, and 
responsiveness to evolving population needs such as ageing, complexity, and substance 
misuse while the NHS Outcomes Framework is introduced, det ailing the domains used to 
measure improvements: preventing premature deaths, enhancing quality of life for those with 
long-term conditions, and supporting recovery from illness or injury.

6.3 NHS Standard Contract 
The NHS Standard Contract is mandated for use by Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) and NHS 
England itself when commissioning non -primary medical services NHS -funded healthcare 
services. Where primary medical services are being commissioned, the appropriate for m of 
primary medical services contract must be used in accordance with the relevant regulations 
and directions. 
In certain circumstances, commissioners may wish to commission a package of services 
including both primary and secondary care elements from a single provider. An example of this 
would be the commissioning of an integrated prisons healthcare service (for w hich the NHS 
Standard Contract must be used) and GP services (for which a general practice contract must 
be used). In those circumstances neither the NHS Standard Contract nor any form of primary 
medical services contract may lawfully be used on its own to  commission that package of 
services. Various contractual structures may be used to deal with this. The use of Schedule 2L 
of the NHS Standard Contract offers a relatively simple solution, for use in appropriate 
circumstances. 
If the package of services includes primary medical services and services for which the NHS 
Standard Contract is the mandated form of contract, commissioners may include provisions in 
Schedule 2L of the NHS Standard Contract to make the Contract compliant with the Alternative 
Provider Medical Services (APMS) Directions in relation to the provision of primary medical 
care services. In other words, to ensure that the contract is both an NHS Standard Contract 
and an APMS contract.  
Schedule 2L is based very closely on NHSE model form of APMS Contract. Both the Standard

7 Core service delivery 
This service is commissioned as part of the overall prison health pathway and as such this 
model will ensure an integrated treatment system both within the prison and onwards into the 
community. The service will focus on delivering person -centred care with in seamless and 
integrated clinical services in prison and facilitating arrangements through the gate into the 
community to ensure effective continuity of care. Close joint working with other healthcare 
services, as well as other departments within the pri son such as education, offender 
management, and physical education, is imperative to the success of the delivery of this 
service.

7.2 Service Aims 
 
The main aims of the healthcare services provided in our male prisons are to: 
• Deliver a trauma -informed service that understands and responds to the gender 
specific physical health issues and emotional well-being of men in prison.  
• Provide a thorough assessment of physical, mental and substance use health needs, 
address immediate needs and make an onward referral to appropriate healthcare 
services. 
•  To ensure there is a pathway in place for screening  for those with Acquired Brain 
Injury improve health outcomes for men in prison and in doing so reduce the drivers of 
reoffending. 
• Assess risk of suicide/self-harm and the impact of coming into prison on emotional and 
mental health and wellbeing. 
• Provide stabilisation of health needs in relation to low mood, acute mental health 
problems, substance misuse needs including alcohol and opiate detoxification /titration 
and physical health needs. 
• Review medication ensuring appropriateness of medication in relation to prison setting 
and health need, whilst working to reduce prescribing for pain relief by providing 
alternative therapies. 
• Robust early screening for learning disabilities, neurodiversity and acquired brain injury 
and other vulnerabilities to ensure appropriate assessment and diagnosis informs the 
support and adjustments made to their care throughout their custodial sentence and 
back out into the community 
• Robust and meaningful planning to support engagement with community -based 
healthcare and related services pre and post release. 
• Robust, flexible and adaptive workforce planning for the future, which is integrated into 
the provider’s financial and business planning.

7.4 Development of digitally enabled care pathways 
• The healthcare provider should develop and optimise using digitally enabled pathways. 
The approach to using digital tools in health care provision is undergoing a substantial and 
rapid shift. Many of the technologies adopted during pandemic were already well established 
but not widely implemented; the maturity of the technology enabled the provision of health 
care, through remote consultation, to be much more prevalent much more quickly. 
Despite this recent rapid adoption of digital technologies, the health and care system remains 
at the early stages of digital health, with many tools replicating physical approaches and 
processes rather than taking advantage of what makes digital different. There are technologies 
on the horizon that are most likely to change health and care over the next few years, but few 
are systematically deployed in the health and care system, and none have reached their full 
potential. Each could represent an opportuni ty to achieve better outcomes or more efficient 
care and improve patient experience. NHS England are keen for providers of healthcare in 
custodial settings to make full use of digital technologies as and when they become available 
to improve outcomes for patients and reduce external escorts.  
The Provider will  also maximise the effective use of digital systems and technology, 
including SystmOne and emerging in -cell technologies where available, alongside 
appropriate administrative support functions. This will support improvements in efficiency, 
release clinical time, and enable staff to focus on the delivery of direct patient care.

7.9 Inclusion criteria  
In carrying out the services the provider will be ‘exercising public functions’ for the purposes 
of section 149(2) of the Equality Act 2010. As such, the service provider must pay due regard 
to the Public Sector Equality Duty under section 149(1) of that Act and to deliver the services 
accordingly. The Equality Act 2010 relates to service users and employees. 
 
The healthcare provider will endeavour to identify and address inequalities in healthcare 
provision and outcomes throughout the duration of the contract.  Their focus should be to 
continuously narrow the health inequalities gap between those in the crimina l justice system 
and the rest of the population and ensure that services are delivered inclusively. This will 
require the provider to collect and maintain complete accurate data sets of the Equalities Act 
2010 protected characteristics. This focus on equality and inclusivity of services is a key thread 
running throughout these service specifications. 
 
The provider must ensure that they have a process in place to identify and capture specific 
datasets relating to service level activity, including but not limited to, patient complaints, 
utilisation of clinics and take up of vaccinations and health screening from individuals from 
ethnic minority backgrounds and LGBT+.  Information on equality of access to services must 
be utilised for service development and as part of the data sets submitted to Commissioners. 
Remedial action must be taken, and appropriate adjustments made to service delivery, to 
ensure equality of healthcare opportunities for each individual service user. 
 
The integrated prison health and social care service will take account of language, cultural 
barriers and bias and focus on early diagnosis of learning disabilities, neurodiversity a nd 
acquired brain injury to ensure enhanced and appropriate support can be given, by all 
stakeholders, throughout their custodial sentence, to those who need it most. The provider will 
strive to reduce health inequalities by achieving a diverse workforce that is representative of 
the population it serves.

7.11 Equivalence  
As required and described in the HSCA 2012  patients within secure settings should receive 
the same quality and access of healthcare as those people in the community – both in terms 
of the range of interventions available to them which meet their needs, and the quality and 
standards of those interventions. The following definition of equivalence has been agreed by 
the national prison health partnership and signed off by the Department of Health and Social 
Care, the Ministry of Justice, HMPPS and NHSE. 
‘Equivalence ‘is the principle which informs the decisions of the National Prison Healthcare 
Board so that member agencies’ statutory and strategic objectives and responsibilities to 
arrange services are met, with the aim of ensuring that people detained in prisons in 
England are afforded provision of and access to appropriate services or treatment (based on 
assessed population need and in line with current national or evidence-based guidelines)

equitable health outcomes and to reduce health inequalities between people in prison and in

Considering the substantial health inequalities likely to be faced by most, if not all, patients 
within secure settings, it is imperative that any provision is not only equitable to community 
provision, but that it takes bold and innovative steps to improve the health of the most 
vulnerable and reduce health inequalities.6

proactive and positive approach to inspection.  
 
The provider will ensure that commissioners, NHSE and HMPPS are kept up to date and 
informed on progress in delivering health improvements to meet Action Plans where relevant.  
 
The provider will work positively with NHSE to develop evidence for CQC (and HMIPS) that 
improvements required are being delivered and are improving the health of the patient 
population. 
7.19 Accountability and oversight 
For all services included in this specification, the provider must ensure that: 
 
• The provider’s Board of Directors is part of the overall clinical governance framework 
with accountability for the quality and performance of all services. 
• The governance structure must provide clarity of the arrangements in place for 
services being delivered by partners or under sub-contract agreements. 
• There are agreed processes in place to track service expenditure. 
• There are internal clinical oversight and assurance with robust operational processes 
in place across all organisations delivering healthcare under this specification. 
• The framework will detail the meetings/forums which are form part of the governance 
arrangements and provide clarity of group membership/quorate from the 
multidisciplinary healthcare team and prison staff. 
• The processes include how the Provider will share learning from  patient safety  
incidents, risks and complaints/compliments. 
7.20 Quality Assurance and Audit 
The Provider must have in place a robust schedule of audit to provide assurance of the quality 
and standard of care being delivered to/with patients. Examples of expected audit include but 
are not limited to records management, infection prevention and control, management of long-
term conditions, patient engagement / DNAs adherence to NICE guidance, pharmacology, 
prescribing and medicines management.

7.21 Policies and Guidance 
 
It is essential that the provider has clear policies and procedures in place to protect patients, 
healthcare and prison staff. These must be regularly reviewed, have clear version control and 
a mechanism for assuring that all staff have read and understood each policy which applies  
to their role. Mechanisms must be in place to ensure that all staff have access to policies, 
processes and standard operating procedures. 
 
7.22 Risk and Incident Management 
The provider must have clear risk and incident management processes which meet national 
standards and consider the needs of the secure setting. The processes must demonstrate 
how they will be open and transparent with patients, Commissioners, the Governors, and  
partner organisations. There should be a central risk register covering all services. It is 
expected that providers will identify risk reduction strategies and investigate those risks which 
are not reducing or fall outside acceptable levels. Staff must have training on risk assessment, 
risk reporting and risk reduction as part of the commitment to patient and staff safety. 
 
The provider will ensure that they have a policy to support the patient safety incident response 
framework (PSIRF), and a patient safety incident response plan (PSIRP). Leaders and staff 
should be appropriately trained in responding to patient safety incid ents including 
investigation. The provider will have process and systems for continuous and sustainable 
improvements in place to learn, improve services and share across systems. Ensure that 
patient safety incident recording systems are compatible with the Learning from Patient Safety 
Events (LFPSE), and responsive to national patient safety alerts. 
 
All staff should be encouraged to report incidents with the provider monitoring these to identify 
trends or areas of concern so that action can be taken to prevent harm to patients and staff. 
This will include the management of control and restraint incidents where the provider will 
ensure adherence to the guidance outlined in In line with current National Patient Safety Alerts, 
NHS England patient safety guidance  and NICE guideline NG10: Violence and aggression: 
short‑term management in mental health, health and community settings, and any subsequent 
updates. It is essential that this includes, clear policies and procedures in place for staff to 
follow which includes the need to monitor, record and act on vital signs during and after all 
restrictive interventions or manual restraints. 
 
7.23 Infection Prevention and Control 
The provider will liaise with the prison Governor to ensure that the necessary mechanisms are 
in place for all healthcare environments to be cleaned on a regular basis. This should include 
an annual deep clean of the clinical areas. To meet infection control standards, in accordance 
with the National Partnership Agreement (2022–2025), the prison Governor is responsible for 
ensuring the availability of an appropriate health care facility. The Governor is also required 
under the agreement to ensure that healthcare facilities are cleaned to NHS standards. 
 
The provider will demonstrate compliance to the Hygiene code within the Health & Social Care 
Act (2008) achieving year on year reductions in Healthcare Associated Infections including 
MRSA and Clostridium difficile. 
 
The Provider will ensure that it has appropriate arrangements for infection prevention control 
and decontamination and that this is compliant with the Health and Social Care Act 2008 
(Code of Practice for the Prevention and Control of Associated Infections).

7.24 Communication 
The Provider MUST COMPLY with the requirements set out within the Accessible Information 
Standard (NHS 2015)  updated in 2025. The Standard directs and defines the specific 
consistent approach to identifying, recording, flagging, sharing and meeting the information 
and communication support needs of patients, service users, carers and parents where those 
needs relate to a disabi lity, impairment or sensory loss. In this specification, this will mean 
ensuring the use of translation services and healthcare literature being made available to 
prisoners and their families in languages other than English. 
 
The provider will have a clear patient communication plan in place that will be refreshed 
annually. There must be robust, effective, inclusive, accessible communication mechanisms 
in place to ensure that patients have consistent, accessible and up to date infor mation on all 
health services to include but not be limited to: 
 
• Information on all healthcare services that are available within the prison, how to 
access them and the care and treatment patients can expect to receive. This 
information must be available in accessible formats, provided using a range of methods 
(including written/pictorial, verbally and digital and utilising in cell technology) and 
located in all areas of the prison (including healthcare, education, workplaces, 
wings/residential units, chaplaincy, library). 
• Provision of on-going, up to date information, located on wings/residential units and in 
healthcare on the days, times and locations of GP/ANP clinics, nurse led clinics, health 
promotion clinics, pharmacy services and medicine administration times. Patients must 
be able to access information of planned clinics at least 6 weeks in advance. 
• Information on Healthcare Complaints process 
• Information on agreed response times and access requirements and expected waiting 
times for all primary care services. 
• Information on the medicines management processes and systems including in 
possession policies. 
• Information on the roles of Health Peer Mentors and how they can assist patients to 
access services. 
 
The provider will work alongside patients and patients’ representatives to ensure that the 
communications plan is meaningful to all patients. The Provider will be required to work with 
NHS England commissioned lived experience organisations (Health councils) in the prison.

8 Health and Justice objectives, outcomes and standards 
The service provider will work in partnership with commissioners and other stakeholders to 
contribute towards the following objectives and outcomes and will consider all opportunities to 
enhance the aims of the service.  
8.1 National collected outcomes  
Each overarching objective has a few specified measures that will be nationally mandated and 
collected nationally for national assurance purposes. The guidance on the national indicators 
will come out annually via an information schedule will which will be sent to providers  by 
regional commissioners. 
8.2 Regional collected measures  
All services should be commissioned to achieve the objectives and their respective outcomes. 
However, how these are achieved will depend upon the service model provided within an 
establishment. Different establishments with differing functions will focus their service on 
achieving the most relevant outcomes for the need of the population. For example, thi s may 
mean that a local reception establishment will have a greater focus on screening and 
assessment and through the gate working, rather than long term treatment interventions. This 
will require local determination by commissioners and providers on priorities based on the 
health needs assessment and the current population.  
To assist with the evaluation against the objectives, the specification incorporates proposed 
regionally driven outcomes that cover the following four domains:
