name: HMP_Winchester_HNA_Detailed_Breakdown.docx
text:
HMP/YOI Winchester
Detailed HNA / EHIA Breakdown for Bid Planning
Prepared for DrPA Secure - ARC model alignment
Source note: The Winchester pack does not appear to contain the full HSCNA/EHIA report as a standalone document. This breakdown is based on the HMP Winchester Information Pack HNA/EHIA summary, Custodial Scorecard, Winchester Service Specification, Social Care Specification and related tender documents supplied in the Winchester pack.
Executive HNA conclusion
HMP/YOI Winchester is not a stable, long-stay planned-care prison. It is a high-churn local reception prison with a large remand and short-stay population, high mental health need, high dual diagnosis, significant substance misuse, social vulnerability, homelessness, disability, neurodiversity and discharge/transfer risk.
The healthcare model therefore needs to be built around:
Front-door control - reception, first night, medicines reconciliation and early risk identification.
Rapid stabilisation - mental health, substance misuse, urgent primary care, IPU and medicines.
Continuity - short-notice release, court movement, transfer, discharge medication and community handover.
Access discipline - clinic utilisation, reduced DNAs, wing-based and EDIC-based follow-up.
Equality and reasonable adjustment - neurodiversity, disability, language, ethnicity, age, homelessness, care leavers and veterans.
This strongly supports the ARC model: Access, Recovery and Continuity.
1. Establishment and population profile
HMP/YOI Winchester is a Category B local prison serving courts across Hampshire and surrounding areas, with a small Category C resettlement unit at West Hill.

What this means
The dominant pressure is throughput. Winchester has a relatively short-stay, high-turnover population. This creates constant demand for reception screening, first-night healthcare, urgent prescribing, medicines reconciliation, mental health risk assessment, substance misuse triage, detoxification and OST continuation, short-notice release planning, rapid discharge summaries and transfer summaries.
The HNA points away from a slow, clinic-only model. The bid must show a high-capacity Access function at the front door.
2. Remand, short stay and release risk
The 57% remand/unsentenced profile is one of the most important HNA findings. Remand prisoners often have unstable community healthcare contact, incomplete medication histories, unresolved mental health and substance misuse needs, high anxiety due to legal uncertainty, increased self-harm and ACCT risk, short-notice court movement, unplanned release, interrupted community prescriptions and housing insecurity.
Bid implication
Describe Winchester as requiring a reception-to-release model, not a custody-only model.
Start release planning at reception, particularly for remand and short-stay residents.
Use named release/transfer coordination, discharge medication tracking and same-day release protocols.
Strengthen GP, community mental health, substance misuse, RECONNECT, probation and housing handover.
3. Mental health need

Mental health is not a niche service at Winchester. It is a core operating pressure across reception, wings, IPU, safer custody and release.
The HNA suggests high demand for rapid triage after referral, ACCT support, trauma-informed interventions, short-term psychological stabilisation, dual diagnosis work, personality disorder-informed practice, ADHD and neurodiversity support, crisis response, IPU mental health input, transfer assessment and discharge summaries.
Bid implication
The mental health model should not be described as a passive referral/waiting-list model. It should be an active in-reach and risk model, with daily duty triage, reception risk flagging, ACCT attendance, IPU input, neurodiversity-informed adjustments, dual diagnosis clinics and release/transfer planning. This justifies the proposed mental health staffing of around 11.9 WTE, including primary mental health, secondary mental health, psychiatry input and neurodiversity/LD capacity.
4. Dual diagnosis
The most important HNA statistic is arguably 48% dual diagnosis. This means almost half of residents have overlapping mental health and substance misuse needs. A split service would create gaps.
Risks if not managed well
People being bounced between mental health and substance misuse teams.
Unmanaged withdrawal worsening mental state.
Self-harm risk during detoxification.
Relapse risk on release.
Trauma and personality disorder presentations being treated as behavioural rather than clinical.
Prescribing risk from sedating, tradable or interacting medicines.
Bid implication
DrPA Secure should operate a joint dual diagnosis pathway across mental health, substance misuse, pharmacy, primary care and safer custody, with shared risk formulation and one integrated care plan for complex patients. This supports the ARC Recovery pathway.
5. Substance misuse need

The caseload is substantial and demand is front-door driven. The low proportion of referrals seen within 5 working days is a key improvement opportunity.
Required service response
Same-day or next-day clinical substance misuse triage.
OST continuation and initiation.
Alcohol withdrawal screening and detoxification.
Daily withdrawal monitoring where required.
Relapse prevention, harm reduction and BBV linkage.
Naloxone planning and community handover.
Joint work with mental health for dual diagnosis.
The C4 incentivised substance-free living landing should be referenced as an opportunity for recovery-focused work, peer-led activity and relapse prevention.
6. Neurodiversity, learning disability and disability

This is a major equality issue. A large proportion of residents will need reasonable adjustments to access healthcare. This affects appointment letters, reception screening, consent, medicines understanding, mental health engagement, substance misuse engagement, health promotion, complaints, dental access and release planning.
Bid implication
Early screening at reception and induction.
Flagging on SystmOne.
Reasonable adjustment plans.
Easy-read healthcare information.
Longer appointment slots where needed.
Wing-based engagement for people who struggle to attend clinics.
Liaison with C1 landing staff.
Staff training in autism, ADHD, LD and acquired brain injury.
7. Homelessness and social vulnerability
The HNA identifies 31% homeless prior to custody. It also flags care leavers and veterans as likely under-identified. Health risk is therefore not limited to clinical diagnoses. Many residents will have unstable housing, low trust in services, poor primary care continuity, poor medication adherence, poverty, trauma and limited social support.
Bid implication
Treat release planning as a clinical safety function.
Identify homelessness risk early.
Link with resettlement, probation, housing partners and RECONNECT.
Confirm community GP, mental health and drug service referral arrangements.
Strengthen safeguarding escalation and support for care leavers/veterans.
8. Medicines management

Reception churn creates a constant medication safety risk because of remand arrivals, short stays, unknown medication histories, tradable medicines, controlled drugs, OST, psychiatric medication, in-possession risk, discharge medication, transfer medication and medicines continuity on release.
Bid implication
Medicines reconciliation linked to reception.
Pharmacist/technician presence in early days.
In-possession risk assessment.
Daily controlled drug governance.
Tradable medicines oversight.
Discharge medication tracking and release medicines dashboard.
Pharmacy input into IPU, mental health and substance misuse.
9. Dental need

Routine dental waits have deteriorated and dental utilisation is not optimal. This suggests regime access constraints, cancellations, movement issues, prioritisation pressure and unmet need.
Bid implication
Urgent dental triage and clinical prioritisation.
Reduced failed appointments through reminders and regime liaison.
Oral health promotion.
Infection prevention and radiography governance.
Clear PDS/tripartite accountability.
Because the tender notes the PDS arrangement, the bid should not imply DrPA directly holds the dental contract unless confirmed. DrPA should retain integration, quality and performance accountability while the dental provider delivers under the PDS/tripartite arrangement.
10. Public health and BBV

Reception testing appears strong, but the wider resident population still needs better reach. Lower total-population Hep C/HCV uptake suggests people not captured at reception, or those needing repeat engagement, may be missed.
Bid implication
The public health model should combine planned screening, vaccination, BBV, sexual health, immunisation, smoking, weight and long-term condition self-management with opportunistic Making Every Contact Count during reception, medication queues, LTC reviews, substance misuse contacts, dental contacts and IPU stays.
11. Long-term conditions, ageing and frailty

Winchester cannot ignore planned care. The high-churn profile creates front-door pressure, but the service still needs safe management of diabetes, respiratory disease, cardiovascular disease, epilepsy, frailty, mobility impairment, pain management and palliative/end-of-life issues where relevant.
Bid implication
Long-term condition register and recall system.
Risk stratification.
Nurse-led clinics with GP/ACP escalation.
Pharmacy optimisation.
Social care links and equipment/reasonable adjustment referrals.
12. Inpatient Unit and urgent care
The pack identifies a 14-15 bed IPU providing 24-hour nursing care and short-term clinical observation. The IPU is a key stabilisation resource for physical health observation, withdrawal/detoxification monitoring, step-up/step-down care, mental health observation where clinically appropriate, frailty and disability support, palliative or complex care where appropriate, and reducing unnecessary external hospital use.
Bid implication
The staffing model must include dedicated IPU nursing and HCA cover. It should not rely solely on generic wing nurses. In ARC terms, the IPU supports Access through urgent admission from reception or wings, Recovery through stabilisation and treatment, and Continuity through safe discharge back to wing, transfer, release or hospital pathway.
13. Social care and disability-related need
The Social Care Specification confirms a separate but integrated social care requirement. Care is delivered in partnership with Hampshire County Council; up to 37.5 hours per week social care support is specified; and social care links to Care Act assessment, Buddy System, personal care, moving and handling, equipment, continence, nutrition, dignity and independence. HCC determines eligibility, but the healthcare provider must integrate care plans and delivery.
Bid implication
Screen for social care indicators at reception.
Refer to Hampshire County Council.
Develop joint care plans and support Buddy System coordination.
Manage moving and handling, equipment requests and clinic access.
Escalate safeguarding risks and plan release for people with care needs.
14. Access, DNAs and regime constraints
Accommodation and enablement constraints contribute to DNA and no-access rates. Winchester has vulnerable prisoner accommodation, a neurodiversity landing, a substance-free living landing, residents with mobility needs, residents needing escort or enablement to clinics, and high reception/court movement.
Bid implication
Daily clinic utilisation review.
Wing-based triage where appropriate.
EDIC follow-up.
Appointment reminders and clinical-risk prioritisation.
Prison regime liaison and escort planning.
DNA review by protected characteristic.
Telemedicine where clinically appropriate.
External appointment tracking.
15. Escorts and bedwatches

The FMT/risk-share documents include a significant Escort & Bedwatch allocation: £555k Year 1 part-year, £740k per full year, £185k final quarter and £5.18m total.
Bid implication
The HNA supports a model that actively reduces avoidable external healthcare activity through stronger urgent care, better IPU use, telemedicine, planned specialist input, better medicines management, proactive long-term condition care, dental triage, better release planning and earlier escalation before deterioration.
16. What the HNA means for the ARC model

17. Staffing implications

The HNA does not support a stripped-back model. It supports an integrated workforce of around 80-85 WTE plus dental, subject to the final financial envelope.
18. Key HNA risks and bid responses

Bottom line for the bid
HMP/YOI Winchester requires a front-door led, trauma-informed and integrated healthcare model that can respond to high churn, remand uncertainty, mental health acuity, dual diagnosis, substance misuse, disability, neurodiversity and short-notice release. DrPA Secure’s ARC model provides this through Access, Recovery and Continuity: rapid assessment and stabilisation at reception, integrated treatment during custody, and safe transfer or release planning from the earliest point.

name: HMP_Winchester_ARC_Bid_Response_Draft_V3_Site_Evidence_CQC.docx
text:
HMP/YOI Winchester Healthcare Bid
Draft Responses - V2 Cross-Checked Against Previous DrPA Secure Bids
ARC Model: Access, Recovery and Continuity
V3 update: site-specific delivery evidence, Oakhill CQC/inspection evidence, corrected Ashtons wording and won/lost bid evidence hierarchy added.
Prepared for DrPA Secure - working draft

1. What has changed in this version
This V2 draft incorporates the uploaded West Yorkshire Men's Prisons responses, Haslar/Campsfield healthcare bid materials and the Winchester ITT pack. It is no longer a generic ARC answer set. The responses now draw on previous DrPA Secure themes, wording logic and evidence examples, while adapting them to the specific Winchester operating context.
The answers have been strengthened with Winchester-specific details: Category B local prison function, small Category C resettlement unit at West Hill, high remand and short-stay population, significant churn, 678 operational capacity, January 2026 snapshot of 627 residents, turnover rate of 3.1 in 2024/25, 57% remand or unsentenced, 14-15 bed IPU, C1 neurodiversity landing, C4 incentivised substance free living landing, two reception clinical rooms, EDIC hub, dedicated dental suite and core day of 7am to 7.30pm.
The financial narrative now reflects the supplied Winchester FMT and Escort & Bedwatch Risk Share Agreement. The confirmed E&BW budget is £555,000 for the initial part-year, £740,000 per full year and £185,000 for the final quarter, totalling £5.18m across the period shown. The provider staffing and subcontractor sections of the supplied FMT copy appear to be unpopulated, so final WTE and price alignment remains a submission-critical check.
2. Source material considered
3. ARC model and FMT control
Access covers reception, first night, urgent triage, medicines reconciliation, early mental health and substance misuse screening, safeguarding, language/communication needs, neurodiversity indicators and 72-hour follow-up.
Recovery covers treatment and stabilisation: primary care, IPU input, mental health, substance misuse, OST and alcohol pathways, pharmacy, dental, long-term conditions, public health, social care interface and multidisciplinary care planning.
Continuity covers planned care, clinics, recalls, external appointments, release and transfer, discharge medicines, social care continuity, probation, RECONNECT, community mental health, community drug and alcohol services and GP/community handover.
The FMT control is essential: the narrative, workforce chart, clinic/session plan, subcontractor model and mobilisation plan must all reconcile to the final FMT. Do not include any role, WTE, session, subcontractor or service commitment that is not funded or commissioned through another route.

3A. V3 evidence update - what has been added
This V3 draft has been updated to reflect the corrected evidence position: East of England and Yorkshire were not won and should be used as internal design learning only, not as proof of delivered services. Delivery proof should now be led by Oakhill, Campsfield, Manston and DrPA Secure subcontracted delivery across NHFT, CNWL and Oxleas sites.
Ashtons should not be described as a site footprint. Ashtons should only be referenced, where relevant, as a pharmacy/medicines relationship or workstream.
The Oakhill evidence has been corrected. Public CQC/Ofsted/HMIP material does not show a simple CQC rating improvement for DrPA. The safer wording is that DrPA took over healthcare at Oakhill in May 2025 and subsequent public inspection evidence records progress in healthcare, including safer healthcare, more staff in place, improved governance structures and greater leadership oversight, while also identifying further work required.
The Winchester bid should therefore avoid saying “DrPA improved the CQC rating at Oakhill” unless separate evidence is available. Use: “public inspection evidence following DrPA mobilisation at Oakhill shows progress in healthcare delivery.”
3B. Corrected evidence hierarchy for Winchester
1. Oakhill - direct award/direct operation, with public inspection evidence showing healthcare progress under DrPA.
2. Campsfield - won secure healthcare contract and mobilisation evidence.
3. Manston - won high-churn healthcare contract, rapid recruitment, surge and mobilisation evidence.
4. NHFT/CNWL/Oxleas subcontractor footprint - evidence of secure healthcare delivery scale across major NHS providers.
5. Site-specific examples - High Down/Highdown, Bronzefield, Bristol, Peterborough and other sites only where DrPA scope and outcome can be evidenced.
6. East of England/Yorkshire bid content - use as internal design learning only, not as delivered service proof.
3C. Oakhill CQC / public inspection evidence - bid-safe summary
CQC lists DrPA Secure - Oakhill Secure Training Centre as provided and run by Doctor PA Ltd, with prison healthcare and caring for children as the relevant service type/specialism. CQC registration includes treatment of disease, disorder or injury and diagnostic/screening procedures.

DrPA Secure will deliver HMP/YOI Winchester through an integrated ARC model: Access, Recovery and Continuity. Access is the front-door and early-days function. This will allow capacity to move across ARC when national policy, drug strategy, population growth or prison expansion changes the risk profile.
The early-days strategy is central to the model. Every new arrival will receive immediate risk screening, medicines reconciliation, and allocation to urgent, enhanced or routine follow-up. Draft response
The substance misuse service will operate within ARC as a rapid access, treatment and recovery pathway. Winchester's profile - high remand and short-stay residents, substance misuse, dual diagnosis, homelessness and significant churn - means the model must prioritise immediate safety, continuity of prescribing and harm reduction while still creating recovery opportunities for those who remain longer.
At reception, all new arrivals will be screened for drug and alcohol risk, including opioid use, alcohol dependence, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, stimulant use, synthetic cannabinoids, poly-drug use, overdose risk, BBV risk, mental health risk and safeguarding. Screening will use appropriate tools and clinical judgement, drawing on the West Yorkshire approach of AUDIT/DUDIT/COWS-style assessment and rapid escalation to prescribing review. OST continuation, OST initiation, alcohol detoxification and urgent withdrawal risks will be prioritised.
The model will adapt to length of stay. For short-stay or remand prisoners, the priority will be safe stabilisation, medicines continuity, harm reduction, naloxone planning where appropriate, BBV testing, advice and rapid community or transfer handover. For longer-stay prisoners, the service will provide structured recovery planning, relapse prevention, psychosocial interventions, health promotion and progression to substance-free/recovery environments where available. Winchester's C4 incentivised substance free living landing provides an important local opportunity for recovery-oriented support.
Treatment will include safe OST prescribing governance, alcohol detoxification, physical health monitoring, BBV screening/vaccination, harm-reduction advice, psychosocial work, motivational interventions, relapse prevention and release planning. Clinical decisions will be made by competent prescribers within agreed protocols and supported by pharmacy governance. Controlled drugs will be managed through supervised administration, diversion prevention, audit and incident learning.
The service will be trauma-informed. Staff will understand that substance misuse may be linked to trauma, adverse childhood experiences, homelessness, exploitation, mental illness, social exclusion and previous interrupted treatment. Interventions will avoid blame, use motivational approaches, recognise shame and stigma, and be adapted for learning disability, neurodiversity, language, literacy and cultural needs.
Dual diagnosis will be managed jointly with mental health and primary care. People will not be passed between services because their presentation is complex. A shared care plan will address withdrawal, medication, mental health, self-harm risk, physical health and release/transfer.
Sufficient staffing will be achieved by using the FMT-funded substance misuse clinical and psychosocial workforce, supported by GP/prescriber/pharmacy input and partner capacity where included. Competence will be maintained through substance misuse training, prescribing supervision, OST governance, alcohol detoxification protocols, safeguarding training, audit, case review and learning from incidents.

Population health intelligence will be drawn from SystmOne, reception data, HNA/Information Pack findings, screening uptake, BBV testing, vaccination, long-term condition registers, substance misuse data, mental health data, IPU activity, dental demand, protected characteristic data where available, complaints, patient feedback and DNAs. The service will use this intelligence to identify priority groups, unmet need and variation in access or outcomes.
Section 7A and other public health programmes will be delivered planned and opportunistically. Reception and induction will be used to offer BBV screening, immunisation review, smoking advice, sexual health signposting, TB/infection risk consideration and health promotion. Planned care will include long-term condition reviews, vaccination, screening signposting, dental prevention, medicines adherence and self-management.
Making Every Contact Count will be built into routine contacts. Nurses, HCAs, mental health staff, substance misuse workers, pharmacy staff, dental staff and care coordinators will reinforce consistent messages on smoking, alcohol, drugs, oral health, sexual health, BBV, sleep, diet, activity, mental wellbeing and medication adherence.
Health inequalities will be reviewed through data and service-user feedback. Particular attention will be paid to young adults, older/frail prisoners, disabled people, neurodiverse prisoners, people with learning disability, people with language needs, people from minority ethnic groups, people who do not self-refer, homeless prisoners and those with dual diagnosis. Reasonable adjustments will include accessible materials, interpretation, outreach, peer support, targeted recalls and flexible appointment arrangements.
Peer and service-user representatives will support health promotion where safe and appropriate, drawing on the West Yorkshire use of peer-led BBV and prevention approaches. Peer activity will be trained, supervised and risk assessed. The aim is a public health model that is data-led, practical and embedded in day-to-day clinical care.

Draft response
Transfer and release planning will sit within the Continuity arm of ARC and will begin at reception. This is essential at Winchester because 57% of the population is reported as remand or unsentenced, creating frequent short-notice changes in status, release and transfer risk. The model is adapted from previous DrPA Secure responses that emphasised continuity of care, medicines, RECONNECT, probation and community handover from the earliest point of custody.
For transfers to another prison or secure hospital, the service will complete transfer summaries and ensure that medication, risk information, ACCT/self-harm concerns, substance misuse treatment, mental health plans, IPU history, long-term conditions, social care needs, safeguarding concerns and outstanding referrals are communicated securely. High-risk transfers will have clinician-to-clinician handover where required.
For release into the community, planning will include medication continuity, GP registration or signposting, mental health referral, substance misuse handover, OST continuity, social care, safeguarding, homelessness risk, probation, RECONNECT and community provider liaison. Particular priority will be given to people with severe mental illness, dual diagnosis, high-risk medication, OST, alcohol dependence, diabetes, respiratory disease, epilepsy, frailty, disability, neurodiversity, homelessness or safeguarding concerns.
Short-notice release will be managed through a rapid continuity protocol. This will prioritise immediate clinical risk, discharge medication, health summary, urgent referrals, harm-reduction advice, naloxone where appropriate, community contact details and escalation to RECONNECT/probation/community services. Where full handover is impossible because release is immediate, actions taken and residual risk will be recorded.
For the West Hill resettlement unit, healthcare will support planned progression, self-management, long-term condition stability and community continuity. For main prison remand and short-stay residents, the pathway will be more rapid and risk-led.
Partnerships will be maintained with probation, RECONNECT, HMPPS, Hampshire County Council/social care, community drug and alcohol services, community mental health, GP/community providers, acute hospitals, VCSE services and housing/homelessness partners where available. These partnerships will be reviewed through operational and quality governance.
Performance will be monitored through release plan completion, discharge medicines, community referral timeliness, failed handovers, urgent post-release incidents, complaints and feedback. This will give commissioners assurance that continuity is a planned clinical safety pathway rather than a late administrative process.
